item.title: TCDA: Tunable Coded Distributed Arrays for Data Availability Sampling
item.description: arXiv:2610.22508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data availability sampling (DAS) lets blockchain nodes verify a block's data availability by downloading only a few random pieces of it. Its network layer must disseminate each block in time for validators to attest (PUT), store it, and serve any piece on request (GET). A trustless DAS must sustain any number of Byzantine peers. The only known design with this guarantee, Robust Distributed Arrays (RDA), achieves it by full replication: each group of nodes responsible for part of a block stores that part in full, so a single good node per group suffices. The price to pay is a PUT load on the critical path to finality that grows with the network and cannot be tuned, hence the data may not reach validators before the attestation deadline. Coding is the natural remedy, but it was not known when a coded layer remains robust against an unbounded adversary, what it costs, or what it gains. We propose TCDA, a coded layer that is provably robust given enough good nodes, wherever they lie, with a tunable knob: how much of its assigned data each node keeps. Turning the knob trades PUT and storage costs against GET cost. It can be set per data type and adjusted as the good-node population changes. At Ethereum's parameters, our evaluation for a 32 MiB block at the recommended uplink shows that RDA misses the attestation deadline at any network size, whereas TCDA can be tuned to meet it from 868 good nodes up to the 40,000 tested, storing 1.7 to 32 times less per node than replication, at the price of 2.5 to 7.7 round-trips per sample instead of about one.
item.dc:creator: Duc A. Tran, Dung Truong, Duy Le

item.title: Fast Distributed $(\Delta + 1)$-Edge Coloring in Bipartite Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.22690v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that, on bipartite $n$-vertex graphs in the LOCAL model of distributed computation, $(\Delta + 1)$-edge coloring can be solved deterministically in $O(f(\Delta) \log n)$ rounds for some function $f$. In particular this implies a deterministic $O(\log n)$-round upper bound for $(\Delta + 1)$-edge coloring on bipartite constant-degree graphs. Our results improve on the previous state-of-the-art bounds (which hold already on general graphs) whose $n$-dependencies are $\widetilde{O}(\log^5 n)$ rounds deterministically and $\widetilde{O}(\log^2 n)$ rounds randomized [Bernshteyn and Dhawan, J.\ Comb.\ Theory 2025]. In fact, we obtain the aforementioned results already for a more restrictive version of $(\Delta + 1)$-edge coloring that corresponds to a \emph{local-palette} strengthening of Vizing's theorem shown recently to hold [Christiansen, STOC 2023]. In this version, every edge $\{u, v\}$ has to be colored with a color from $\{1, \dots, \max(\operatorname{deg}(u), \operatorname{deg}(v))+ 1\}$. For all of our results, the vertices do not need to know on which side of the bipartition they lie---the structural promise of bipartiteness suffices.
item.dc:creator: Yann Bourreau, Sebastian Brandt, Ananth Narayanan

item.title: Accelerated Dataflow: scaling inference in streaming data analytics with efficiency
item.description: arXiv:2610.22731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Streaming data analytics helps businesses identify opportunities and spot risks in a timely fashion. As large language model (LLM) usage grows, people are exploring incorporating agents or LLMs in streaming data pipelines to help find patterns in datasets without supervision or interpret natural languages for content moderation. However, most streaming systems are currently optimized for data movement and perform poorly on GPU intensive workloads such as performing inference with LLMs. We introduce a system on Google Cloud Dataflow designed to tackle hybrid streaming machine learning workloads with co-designed autoscaling on heterogeneous worker pools and prefix-aware batching. This increases throughput 1.5x to 2x for streaming pipelines using LLMs while maintaining similar latency with up to 75% peak resource savings and 84% lower peak tail latency compared with existing streaming data processing systems.
item.dc:creator: RuiLong Jiang, Dustin Rhodes, Danny McCormick, Yuta Labur, Reza Rokni

item.title: One Communicator, Three Vendors: Extending the MoA Predictive Theory to a Real NVIDIA+AMD+CPU MPI Ensemble
item.description: arXiv:2610.22769v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The companion MPI-extension paper validated the first communication-bearing machine-shape ensemble: four NVIDIA A100 ranks and four CPU ranks on one NCSA Delta node under one Open MPI job, reassembled by MPI_Gatherv. This paper extends it to a multi-vendor communicator. A Slurm heterogeneous job spanning Delta's A100 and AMD MI100 partitions places A100, MI100 and CPU ranks (nine in all) under one communicator for the first time. We give the theory (a w_i proportional to 1/t_i weight split for three concurrent realizations; a het-job specification as an admissible directive) and report real results, including what the run exposed: the 1/t split assumes time linear in rows, and this fails for the MI100 rank (6 rows took 597 ms against a linear prediction of 1.6 ms). A launch-geometry model, with predictions recorded before measuring, succeeds for the A100 (time flat from 128 to 3456 rows, stepping at exactly 3520 and 6976) and places the MI100 floor in the key loop; changing its launch settings cut about 600 ms to 14.6 ms and the energy per call at 6 rows by 32x, though the MI100 remains about 95x slower than an A100 at 8192 rows. Controlled reruns show that the companion paper's 8.1x A100 result and 22 ms Gatherv were artifacts of four ranks sharing one GPU under Open MPI's default transport. A key/value-split partition whose message sizes are derived from shapes alone is then run: the ring Allreduce of the 8.5 MB message took 11.3, 16.0 and 15.3 ms against a predicted 11-12 ms, the small Allreduce missed its prediction in every run, and compute times reproduce to about 1% while communication times vary up to 4x between runs. Each idea is introduced with a figure and closed with worked examples.
item.dc:creator: Lenore Mullin, Gaetan Hains

item.title: Understanding KV Residency in Production-Scale Agentic LLM Workloads
item.description: arXiv:2610.22863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic large language model (LLM) applications turn one user request into a sequence of model and tool calls over a growing context. Retaining this context's key-value (KV) state in GPU memory lets later calls reuse it instead of recomputing it, but at fleet scale this needs substantial memory. We characterize four production Microsoft M365 workload traces (Deep Research, Enterprise Assistant, Coding Agent and Enterprise Chat) spanning more than 121 million model calls. In Deep Research, the application issues 89% of model calls and the median context grows from about 10K to 68K tokens by the 30th call. About 80% of context tokens are served from the prefix cache. With the public Llama-2-70B KV layout standing in for confidential models, one 99th-percentile Deep Research session exceeds the 80 GB HBM of an NVIDIA H100, and holding all live sessions at their peak needs an estimated 501.8 TB of HBM, although inference occupies only 5.6% of that retention time. Trace-driven replay shows that a one-hour idle cap cuts this ceiling by 3.6x while raising the share of calls that recompute context only from 4.07% to 4.53%. Under tighter budgets, eviction alone is insufficient: at one tenth of the busiest hour's demand, LRU eviction makes 63% of Deep Research calls recompute and clairvoyant furthest-next-use 31%, whereas multi-resolution retention (MRR), which demotes the LRU session's KV state to int4, lowers this to 13.6%. Placement imposes a separate limit: when the next call reaches a different deployment, cached-context reuse drops from 89% to 29%, and treating KV state as deployment-local raises the recompute floor under unlimited memory from 5.4% to 20.2%. These findings motivate retention that changes the representation of KV state, together with deployment-aware routing or migration. We plan to release AgenticTraceSim, a parametric trace generator, and a residency replay framework.
item.dc:creator: Mayank Arya, Agrim Bari, Anjaly Parayil, Yogesh Simmhan, Renee St. Amant, Victor R\"uhle, Saravan Rajmohan

item.title: MailRail: Mitigating Incast Congestion with User-Space, Node-Based Flow Control
item.description: arXiv:2610.22890v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Irregular workloads, such as those stemming from Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, frequently induce severe incast congestion in large-scale parallel environments. Existing fabric-level congestion control mechanisms rely on reactive, link-level rate limiting that degrades overall throughput. While receiver-driven, credit-based flow control offers a proactive alternative, as process counts scale memory slots per rank fall below usable thresholds, rendering traditional rank-based accounting untenable. To address this challenge, we introduce MailRail, an out-of-order, asynchronous messaging framework, along with a novel user-space, node-based credit flow control system. By shifting credit accounting from individual processes to shared per-node pools, our proactive, fabric-agnostic approach maintains sufficient credit availability even as process density grows, enabling processes to dynamically utilize freed credits without waiting for receiver-side redistribution. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that node-based flow control achieves up to a 1132x speedup over unconstrained execution at an adversarial incast ratio of 4096:1 while adding minimal overhead on uniform workloads.
item.dc:creator: Noel Gomillion, Lance Fletcher, Trevor Steil, Eun Jung Kim, Roger Pearce

item.title: QuarkShard: Decomposing Cross-Shard Requests into Single-Input Transactions
item.description: arXiv:2610.23014v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sharding blockchains enhance scalability by distributing the workload across multiple shards. Within sharding blockchains, securely and efficiently processing cross-shard user requests remains a pivotal challenge. Traditional sharding blockchain protocols execute cross-shard requests under a processing paradigm that treats each user request as a monolithic entity to preserve its atomicity, inherently introducing significant intra-shard BFT execution overhead and cross-shard communication overhead. We propose QuarkShard, a sharding protocol that breaks away from this traditional paradigm to achieve intra-shard and cross-shard overheads below the lower bounds imposed by conventional approaches. QuarkShard decomposes cross-shard requests into single-input-shard transactions, where each transaction requires consensus and processing within only a single shard, thereby substantially reducing total request processing overhead. Meanwhile, through a carefully designed request decomposition algorithm, QuarkShard guarantees fund atomicity or location atomicity during request execution. QuarkShard also enhances the security of blockchain sharding systems against MEV attacks and flooding attacks. Empirical evaluation across a wide-area network spanning four AWS regions demonstrates that QuarkShard achieves superior performance, attaining a peak throughput of $1024$k requests per second with sub-$4$-second latency. Benchmark comparisons show that QuarkShard achieves up to $210.7\%$ and $314.8\%$ of the maximum throughputs of Kronos and 2PC, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Changyu Duan (Tsinghua University), Zhixuan Fang (Tsinghua University)

item.title: DIFFLET: A Fast Inference Engine for Diffusion Transformer Models on AWS Trainium
item.description: arXiv:2610.23047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On AWS Trainium2, every component of a diffusion model runs as a program compiled ahead of time for fixed shapes, while pipelines differ across models, prompt lengths across requests, and caching decisions across denoising steps. We present Difflet, a serving engine in which five model pipelines share one compilation backend, joint attention is split across cores by attention head, and a host controller decides at each denoising step whether to run the denoiser or reuse its earlier output. A small probe program computes the caching signal on the device and returns one number per step, and a resident model process keeps every program loaded across requests. Across five image and video model families, fused attention accelerates denoiser steps by 1.2-4.3x over the same framework using PyTorch/XLA attention, and at 32.8k visual tokens it is the only attention that compiles. On four of the five models, resident serving is 1.5-3.4x faster than standalone runs that reload weights from a warm file cache for each generation.
item.dc:creator: Bin Ma, Min Yu, Vijay Kodamalla, Jialin Liu, Dong Li

item.title: BaGuaLu-2: Taming Dynamic Memory Fluctuation for Efficient MoE Model Training over 10,000 GPUs
item.description: arXiv:2610.23064v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is the de facto architecture for scaling large language models. However, dynamic expert load imbalance causes severe memory fluctuations that degrade training efficiency. Existing systems rely on static memory provisioning: they either over-provision, leaving GPU memory idle during normal execution, or under- provision, inviting out-of-memory crashes and costly manual rollbacks when load spikes occur. To address these challenges, we propose BaGuaLu-2, a large-scale MoE training system that eliminates this dilemma through flexible provisioning. By transforming memory allocation from a static, one-time tuning choice into a continuous and fine-grained control. BaGuaLu-2 grants exact activation memory on demand for each training batch. Furthermore, it offsets any dynamic management overhead through system optimizations. BaGuaLu-2 demonstrates exceptional scalability, training a model with 1040 billion parameters across 12,288 GPUs while sustaining over 2 EFlops at 35% MFU. Compared with state-of-the-art systems, BaGuaLu-2 delivers 1.14x and 1.13x average throughput improvements over Megatron-Kuai and AdaPipe, respectively.
item.dc:creator: Mingshu Zhai, Minkun Guo, Hongrui Lian, Shuangyu Li, Qi Zhang, Chen Hu, Xiawei Du, Yuyang Jin, Zan Zong, Jidong Zhai

item.title: On the Power of Alternating Local Certification with Constant-Size Certificates
item.description: arXiv:2610.23694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study alternation hierarchies for distributed decision in anonymous networks with constant-size certificates. A prover and a disprover alternately assign certificates to nodes over a constant number of rounds, after which each node decides whether to accept based on its own input and the certificates observed in its neighborhood. An instance is accepted if all nodes accept. Unlike previous work on distributed alternation hierarchies, which considered restricted local computation (Reiter, PODC 2024) or logarithmic-size certificates (Feuilloley et al., ICALP 2016), we focus on constant-size certificates and the role of neighborhood information in determining expressive power. We consider three models: SET, where nodes observe only the set of certificate sequences of their neighbors; MULTISET, where multiplicities are also visible; and PORTS, where neighbors can additionally be distinguished by local port numbers. We establish that SET is strictly weaker than MULTISET, which is in turn strictly weaker than PORTS, and that all three alternation hierarchies are strict at every level. Despite their severe restrictions, these models are remarkably expressive: LEADER belongs to the third level of SET. Our main characterization shows that, over finite input alphabets, SET coincides exactly with monadic second-order logic (MSO$_1$). Moreover, every language definable in counting monadic second-order logic (CMSO$_1$) belongs to PORTS, while MULTISET already contains languages that are not CMSO$_1$-definable. Nevertheless, this expressive power has fundamental limitations. PORTS does not capture MSO$_2$: neither Hamiltonicity nor the existence of a perfect matching belongs to PORTS. Furthermore, over unbounded input alphabets, PORTS cannot verify that every node has been given the correct network size.
item.dc:creator: Pedro Montealegre, Mart\'in R\'ios-Wilson, Jukka Suomela, Guillaume Theyssier

item.title: TRACE: Transformer Residual Activation Codebook Encoding for Communication-efficient Distributed Edge Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.22435v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Distributed Transformer inference across co-located edge devices is fundamentally communication-bound, as exchanging activations between sequence-parallel partitions dominates inference latency under commodity edge bandwidths. Existing compression schemes reduce this cost but retain a structural bottleneck: the received data must still undergo key/value projection before attention can proceed, serializing computation behind communication. This paper presents Transformer Residual Activation Codebook Encoding (Trace), a framework that addresses these limitations. Trace places a Vector Quantizer (VQ) at the post-attention residual of every Transformer layer and precomputes codebook-indexed key/value representations. During inference, exchanged activations are encoded into compact codebook indices, allowing receivers to directly recover keys and values through table lookup instead of executing the downstream computations required to derive them. By eliminating the received data downstream computation, Trace enables communication--computation overlap and reduces a key latency bottleneck in distributed Transformer inference. A hierarchical clustering further structures the learned codebook into a multi-resolution hierarchy, enabling runtime adaptation of the communication bitrate without retraining. The framework supports two operating variants: one prioritizing accuracy and the other balancing accuracy and efficiency through buffer-compatible quantization. Experiments on ViT-Base (ImageNet-1K and CIFAR-100) and ViViT-B (UCF-101) show that Trace achieves up to 1.89% higher accuracy and up to 1.27x end-to-end inference speedup compared with the state-of-the-art VQ-based distributed inference framework. Compared with uncompressed sequence-parallel inference, Trace reduces communication overhead by up to 22,624x.
item.dc:creator: Muhammad Azlan Qazi, Alexandros Iosifidis, Qi Zhang

item.title: The LLM-Attacker: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.22722v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attacker, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here, it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.
item.dc:creator: Georgios Politis, Evangelos Pappas

item.title: FederatedBytes: Tokenizer-Free, Byte-Level Small Language Models for Efficient Multimodal Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.22906v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) is a powerful machine learning framework that allows building a global model from the contributions of multiple, distributed clients, while ensuring the privacy of their local data. However, its heavy computational and communication overheads challenge its use for contemporary AI workloads such as natural language processing (NLP) and multimodal analysis. For this reason, this paper presents a novel small language model that leverages byte-level text and multimodal data processing, enhanced by a linear attention mechanism, to enable manageable Federated Learning of NLP and multimodal analysis tasks. The proposed model, nicknamed FederatedBytes, manages to process text and any other data types, including images, by treating its input as a mere sequence of bytes, while its lean linear attention mechanism allows abating the overall memory and computational footprint. To prove the effectiveness of the proposed model we have carried out an extensive performance evaluation on sentiment analysis tasks in multilingual and multimodal settings over the Multilingual Amazon Reviews and ScienceQA datasets. The experimental results show that FederatedBytes has been able to outperform comparable models such as ByT5 and LSTM, achieving higher accuracy while significantly reducing memory and communication overheads.
item.dc:creator: Ali Sarabadani, Massimo Piccardi, Mehran Abolhasan, Farzad Tofigh, Ian Zhou, Justin Lipman

item.title: Scalable Levenberg-Marquardt Training Framework for Deep Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.22925v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Levenberg-Marquardt (LMA) algorithm is a widely used nonlinear least-squares solver known for its rapid convergence. For small-scale neural networks, LMA provides better convergence and architectural robustness than first-order optimizers like Adam. However, LMA imposes prohibitive memory and computational costs. These costs are primarily from the Jacobian matrix, whose dimensions scale with both the number of samples and parameters. This bottleneck prevents its use in large-scale neural networks. Recent efforts scale LMA using preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) solvers to avoid materializing the Jacobian. However, PCG only approximates the solution, requiring many network propagations and a task-specific preconditioner. Other studies optimize LMA to reduce costs, but they restrict their methods to specific tasks or network architectures. As a result, LMA remains impractical for training general large-scale neural networks. In this paper, we propose LeMA, a distributed LMA algorithm for large-scale neural network training on multi-GPU platforms. Our contributions are twofold: First, an exact dual formulation of LMA removes the memory dependence on the parameter dimension. Second, a Jacobian sharding strategy computes Jacobian shards on the fly and in parallel to avoid materializing the full Jacobian. For large-scale neural networks, LeMA reduces the memory footprint of LMA from quadratic in the number of parameters to quadratic in the batch size. This makes exact LMA steps feasible for billion-parameter models without approximate PCG solves. Furthermore, for a convolutional neural network with 1,000,022,632 parameters on an 8-GPU node, LeMA achieves a 7.97x speedup over a single GPU, corresponding to a 99.7% strong scaling efficiency.
item.dc:creator: Xianghao Wang, Johan Barth\'elemy, John Taylor

item.title: Encodings and Node Architecture: Lessons from the Fault-Tolerant Distributed Transversal Fanout
item.description: arXiv:2610.22966v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: An encoding choice specifies the quantum error-correcting code used to encode logical qubits at a given node. Different encoding choices may differ in the number of physical qubits, the number of encoded logical qubits, the code distance, and the available fault-tolerant operations. We study different encodings for a distributed transversal fanout operation and look at its implications on node architecture. Our experiments suggest that an encoding with higher distance, even if requiring more ebits, can yield a lower logical error rate for distributed operations, and that ``upgrading'' an encoding prior to distributed operations and having a cache, as part of node architecture, for qubits can be useful for distributed operations.
item.dc:creator: Seng W. Loke

item.title: TALLOP: Joint Optimization of Local Training and Communication Compression for Time-Constrained Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2610.22996v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Minimizing the wall-clock time required to reach a target accuracy is crucial in federated learning (FL), where many applications require frequent model updates as data distributions evolve over time. Nevertheless, in heterogeneous environments, slow clients with limited computational and communication capabilities can delay global synchronization, forcing faster clients to wait and increasing the overall training time. To mitigate this straggler effect, recent studies have introduced per-round time constraints and adapted client workloads within the available time. However, these approaches primarily focus on local computation, whereas communication can become a major bottleneck in communication-limited environments, motivating the joint optimization of training workload and communication compression. Although previous studies have explored such joint optimization, determining an effective training--communication balance under a fixed per-round time budget remains challenging, as the resulting model performance depends on both training progress and compression-induced degradation. We therefore propose TALLOP, which jointly optimizes the local training workload and communication compression under per-round time constraints. TALLOP predicts the training loss achievable under different computation budgets from the early-stage mini-batch loss trajectory (LENS), and estimates the degradation caused by communication compression using a compression-error model (CLEN). TALLOP combines these predictions to select the training-communication allocation that minimizes the post-compression loss under the given round time constraint. Experiments in heterogeneous FL environments show that TALLOP generally achieves competitive or improved time-to-accuracy compared with approaches that optimize only local training or neither, although the benefit over training-only adaptation depends on the setting.
item.dc:creator: Honoka Anada, Yafei Ou, Shinya Takamaeda-Yamazaki

item.title: ScaleRAN: A Runtime for Elastic GPU Resource Management in AI-RAN
item.description: arXiv:2610.23072v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI-RAN is driving the convergence of radio access network (RAN) processing and artificial intelligence (AI) workloads on GPU-enabled computing platforms, ranging from GPU-accelerated base stations to cloud-native infrastructures. While GPU acceleration improves the efficiency of virtualized RAN functions, the computational demand of latency-critical baseband processing varies with traffic load, creating transient spare GPU capacity that can be reclaimed by co-located AI applications. Existing GPU-sharing mechanisms rely on coarse-grained hardware partitioning or static resource allocation, limiting their ability to adapt to slot-level workload fluctuations while preserving strict timing requirements. This paper presents ScaleRAN, a node-local runtime for elastic GPU resource management in AI-RAN. ScaleRAN leverages NVIDIA Green Contexts to dynamically partition Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) between RAN and AI workloads through a ladder of pre-created GPU partitions, enabling low-overhead resource reallocation at RAN slot granularity. The proposed runtime naturally supports Open-RAN (O-RAN) O-Cloud deployments, one representative AI-RAN deployment scenario. To drive these reallocations, we propose a reactive controller inspired by Kubernetes autoscaling and a proactive controller based on quantile regression and conformal prediction. We also develop LDPCSim, a GPU-accelerated workload generator built on NVIDIA Aerial for reproducible evaluation. Results show that predictive fine-grained GPU partitioning satisfies slot-level RAN deadlines while increasing the GPU resources available to co-located AI workloads, demonstrating the practicality of elastic GPU sharing for future AI-RAN platforms.
item.dc:creator: Arthur Hamard, J\'er\'emie Leguay, Gopalasingham Aravinthan, Alberto Conte, Julien Lallet, Abdelkader Outtagarts

item.title: On the (In)stability of Adaptive Fee Mechanisms in Multi-Chain Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.23305v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: EIP-1559 has become the dominant transaction fee mechanism in permissionless blockchains, regulating scarce block space through an adaptive base fee. The design balances a trade-off between responsiveness to demand fluctuations and stability of long-term resource usage. On a single chain, this trade-off is well understood and empirically stable. In multi-chain systems, however, cross-chain flows introduce delayed economic interactions across otherwise independent fee markets. These interactions alter the control dynamics and create stability risks that existing models do not capture. Deployed systems have already polarized. Polkadot enforces conservative update rates, effectively disabling fee adaptivity and reverting the market to inefficient first-price auctions. Cosmos adopts aggressive update rates without formal guarantees. To fill this gap, we propose a control-theoretic framework that formalizes multi-chain fee markets as a nonlinear dynamical system with delayed feedback. We identify delay-amplified over-correction as the structural root of instability. Experiments show that cross-chain coupling erodes stability relative to monolithic blockchains, reducing the safe parameter space for base fee update rates by up to 84.8%. Moreover, instability propagates across chains, contaminating the otherwise stable peer chains. At Ethereum's update rate, which leaves a monolithic chain stable, the multi-chain system exhibits extreme load oscillation between full and near-empty blocks, with over half of all blocks at full capacity. Mainstream Cosmos chains already exceed their safe bounds under their default configurations, and the resulting load oscillation raises their block failure rate by an order of magnitude. Guided by this mechanism, we design a lightweight protocol-level mitigation that removes the over-correction and stabilizes dynamics in multi-chain environments.
item.dc:creator: Yifan Zhou, Jiang Xiao, Xuechao Wang, Ru Cheng, Shijie Zhang

item.title: From Border-Agnosticism to Causal Rewrite Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.23351v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Causal Graph Rewriting was recently introduced as an evolution of Causal Graph Dynamics to allow for a controlled form of asynchronism in these dynamical systems with dynamical graphs. In this context, the notion of borders---akin to dangling edges---has gained increasing importance. In this paper, we re-examine these borders, interpreting them as missing information. This perspective adds structural rigor to the framework, allowing border-agnostic causal graph rewriting to be reformulated as a rewriting system rather than a dynamical system. This shift represents a crucial step toward facilitating the treatment of reversibility.
item.dc:creator: Pablo Arrighi, Marin Costes, Luidnel Maignan

item.title: Flash RNN-T: Memory-Efficient Joint Network and Transducer Loss Computation
item.description: arXiv:2610.23409v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The recurrent neural network transducer (RNN-T) remains a practical choice for streaming speech recognition, but training requires large intermediate tensors. We present Flash RNN-T, a joint and loss implementation combining specialized kernels with optional tiled recomputation over the full alignment space and vocabulary. Tiled and untiled Flash form the entire measured throughput-memory frontier on medium and long workloads. On H100, untiled Flash achieves 24-39% higher throughput with 26-56% less memory than the fastest baseline on these workloads wherever it fits. Tiling reduces memory further through recomputation. On medium, tiled Flash uses ninefold less memory than that baseline at 16% lower throughput when both use one backward call per batch. On long, it fits where all tested alternatives with that backward schedule run out of memory with 80 GB. These comparisons use each implementation's lowest-memory configuration reaching at least 95% of its peak throughput.
item.dc:creator: Mahmoud Ashraf

item.title: Agentic AI for Heterogeneous System Design Across Chip, Scale-Up, and Scale-Out Domains
item.description: arXiv:2610.23724v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The design space of modern AI/HPC systems has expanded rapidly across compute architectures, including GPUs, dataflow processors, and RISC-V accelerators; memory tech- nologies, including HBM, GDDR, and SRAM; and interconnects such as NVLink, UALink, Infinity Fabric, InfiniBand, Slingshot, and Ultra Ethernet. No single architecture is optimal across LLM training, LLM serving, and AI-coupled HPC workloads, while the resulting combinatorial design space is too large for manual exploration. We present ArchAgent, a hierarchical multi- agent framework in which an LLM-based planner decomposes system design into chip, scale-up, and scale-out subproblems, each handled by specialist agents. A deterministic analytical evaluator closes the loop, ensuring that all performance estimates are derived from analytical models rather than generated by the LLM. On a mixed AI+HPC workload under a 1 MW power budget, ArchAgent discovers heterogeneous designs that achieve a 1.93x weighted geometric mean speedup over a homogeneous GPU baseline, while requiring only 18 evaluations compared with 100 evaluations for hill climbing, which achieves 1.65x speedup.
item.dc:creator: Murali Emani, Kashyap R Manjusha

item.title: Federated k-Core Decomposition: A Secure Distributed Approach
item.description: arXiv:2410.02544v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As one of the most well-studied cohesive subgraph models, the $k$-core is widely used to find graph nodes that are ``central'' or ``important'' in many applications, such as biological networks, social networks, ecological networks, and financial networks. For Decentralized Online Social Networks (DOSNs), where each vertex is a client as a single computing unit, distributed k-core decomposition algorithms have already been proposed. However, current distributed approaches fail to adequately protect privacy and security. In today's data-driven world, data privacy and security have attracted more and more attention, e.g., DOSNs are proposed to protect privacy by storing user information locally without using a single centralized server. In this work, we are the first to propose the secure version of the distributed $k$-core decomposition.
item.dc:creator: Bin Guo, Emil Sekerinski, Lingyang Chu

item.title: Optimistic, Signature-Free Reliable Broadcast and Its Applications
item.description: arXiv:2505.02761v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reliable broadcast (RBC) is a key primitive in fault-tolerant distributed systems, and improving its efficiency can benefit a wide range of applications. This work focuses on signature-free RBC protocols, which are particularly attractive due to their computational efficiency. Existing protocols in this setting incur an optimal 3 steps to reach a decision while tolerating up to $f < n/3$ Byzantine faults, where $n$ is the number of parties. In this work, we propose an optimistic RBC protocol that maintains the $f < n/3$ fault tolerance but achieves termination in just 2 steps under certain optimistic conditions--when at least $\lceil \frac{n+2f-2}{2} \rceil$ non-broadcaster parties behave honestly. We also prove a matching lower bound on the number of honest parties required for 2-step termination. We show that our latency-reduction technique generalizes beyond RBC and applies to other primitives such as asynchronous verifiable secret sharing (AVSS) and asynchronous verifiable information dispersal (AVID), enabling them to complete in 2 steps under similar optimistic conditions. To highlight the practical impact of our RBC protocol, we integrate it into Sailfish++, a new signature-free, post-quantum secure DAG-based Byzantine fault-tolerant (BFT) consensus protocol. Under optimistic conditions, this protocol achieves a commit latency of 3 steps--matching the performance of the best signature-based protocols. Our experimental evaluation shows that our protocol significantly outperforms existing post-quantum secure and signature-based protocols, even on machines with limited CPU resources. In contrast, signature-based protocols require high CPU capacity to achieve comparable performance. We have open-sourced our Rust implementation of Sailfish++ to facilitate reproducible results.
item.dc:creator: Nibesh Shrestha, Qianyu Yu, Aniket Kate, Giuliano Losa, Kartik Nayak, Xuechao Wang

item.title: RoutePack: Replay-Guided Expert Placement and Rollout Trajectory Scheduling for MoE Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2608.12146v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models couples two load-balancing problems. Rollout-trajectory composition determines attention and dense feed-forward work across data-parallel (DP) replicas, while token routing determines expert work across expert-parallel ranks. Optimizing either side independently can worsen the other. Routing replay exposes trajectory lengths and layer-wise expert demand before training, creating an opportunity to coordinate both controls. We present RoutePack, a replay-guided planner that coordinates expert placement and rollout-trajectory scheduling. Its key insight is that placement determines a batchwise expert-rank load bound that trajectory scheduling alone cannot lower, while scheduling controls the hotspots within individual execution micro-steps. RoutePack incrementally adjusts expert placement while preserving expert residency, then uses parallel population annealing to reschedule complete trajectories into token-capped microbatches. Its objective jointly balances dense-side work and layer-wise expert peaks under a fixed, capacity-feasible micro-step count and the deployed synchronization groups. The planner preserves logical token routing and keeps placement fixed throughout forward and backward execution to maintain training-state consistency. We evaluate mixed-task RL post-training of two hybrid-attention MoE models (7.9B and 124B parameters) across six NVIDIA H20-3e configurations spanning 8K-32K contexts. Within the Megatron training region, RoutePack achieves 4.44-11.85% higher throughput than a DP-local first-fit-decreasing baseline and 1.33-5.28% higher throughput than expert rerouting alone. Additional evaluations of the 7.9B model on H200 and H20 retain positive gains. We separately characterize planning and admission costs.
item.dc:creator: Yibo Shen, Xudong Han, Xiaowei Zhu, Gen Li, Zhenxuan Pan

item.title: From Pilots to Production: Lessons in Cross-Institutional Federated Training and Artificial Intelligence for Science
item.description: arXiv:2609.39803v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many of the most valuable scientific datasets cannot be centralized: they are proprietary, export-controlled, classified, or bound by data-sovereignty restrictions. This inverts the usual paradigm: the model must move to the data, making federated artificial intelligence (AI) core infrastructure for open science. We synthesize lessons from U.S. Department of Energy national laboratories, industry deployments, and the open-source community into a structured account of moving federated AI from pilot demonstrations to dependable, multi-site production. The lessons come from five concurrent efforts spanning leadership-class supercomputers and cloud infrastructure in regulated settings. We organize them around an adapted \textit{five-domain readiness frame} and a stratified view of the stack beneath a trained model: data architecture, privacy and security controls, trust and verification, governance and socio-technical factors, and operations, the layers that decide whether a pilot becomes dependable. The question shifts from ``can we train it?'' to ``can we operate it, audit it, and change it safely?'' We report systems lessons in memory efficiency, reliability, and synchronization; set out what privacy, security, and decentralized trust require in production, and what is not yet validated there; and identify cross-cutting open problems (asynchronous federation, leakage auditing, verification standards, and harmonized data contracts) that we argue warrant a dedicated, international, open-science working group.
item.dc:creator: Olivera Kotevska, Max Carlson, Yan Gao, Francis Jeanson, Yijiang Li, Mohammad Naseri, Minseok Ryu, Sahil Tyagi, Jerry Watkins, Feiyi Wang, Ravi Madduri, Kibaek Kim

item.title: Revisiting Cauchy-Schwarz Norm Bounds for SDC Detection in LLM Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.18557v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) execute billions of floating-point operations per output token across many hardware accelerators. At this scale, hardware-induced faults can bypass system-level detection mechanisms and cause Silent Data Corruption (SDC). Algorithm-Based Fault Tolerance (ABFT) is the state-of-the-art technique for protecting matrix multiplication from such faults, but it incurs non-negligible computational overhead and requires thresholds to distinguish hardware-induced errors from floating-point roundoff. In this paper, we revisit Cauchy--Schwarz Norm Bounds (CSNB) as a low-overhead alternative for detecting SDC during LLM inference. We compare CSNB against ABFT through controlled fault injection and evaluate the runtime overhead of both verification and threshold determination across multiple model sizes, batch sizes, and generation lengths. Our results show that, on average, CSNB retains 99% of the fault detection capability of ABFT for the evaluated linear layers in dense LLMs, while reducing verification overhead by 87% and threshold determination overhead by 67%. For Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router gate computations, however, CSNB retains only 55% of the fault detection capability of ABFT. These findings suggest that CSNB is a promising low-overhead alternative for protecting linear layers in dense LLMs, while checksum-based verification remains preferable for the evaluated MoE router gate.
item.dc:creator: Anton Altenbernd, Dylan Everingham, Philipp Wiesner, Odej Kao

item.title: Distributed Stochastic Momentum Tracking with Local Updates: Achieving Optimal Communication Complexities
item.description: arXiv:2510.24155v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose Local Momentum Tracking (LMT), a novel distributed stochastic gradient method for solving distributed optimization problems over networks. To reduce communication overhead, LMT enables each agent to perform multiple local updates between consecutive communication rounds. Specifically, LMT integrates local updates with the momentum tracking strategy and the Loopless Chebyshev Acceleration (LCA) technique. We demonstrate that LMT achieves linear speedup with respect to the number of local updates as well as the number of agents for minimizing smooth objective functions with and without the Polyak-{\L}ojasiewicz (PL) condition. In particular, LMT outperforms existing distributed stochastic gradient methods with local updates, and notably attains the optimal communication complexities with sufficiently many local updates $Q\geq Q^*$. For a moderate number of local updates $Q=\mathcal{O}(1)$, the performance of LMT matches the best known result for $Q=1$ under smooth nonconvex objectives, and improves upon it under the PL condition. For $Q=1$, we further establish minimax performance lower bounds over two comparison families. For smooth objectives, LMT matches the lower bound. For PL objectives, LMT attains the minimax-optimal dependence on the spectral gap, up to logarithmic factors. To our knowledge, LMT is the first distributed stochastic gradient method with local updates that enjoys such properties.
item.dc:creator: Kun Huang, Shi Pu

item.title: Accelerated Execution of Bayesian Neural Networks using a Single Probabilistic Forward Pass and Code Generation
item.description: arXiv:2511.23440v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Machine learning models perform well across domains such as diagnostics, weather forecasting, NLP, and autonomous driving, but their limited uncertainty handling restricts use in safety-critical settings. Traditional neural networks often fail to detect out-of-domain (OOD) data and may output confident yet incorrect predictions. Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) address this by providing probabilistic estimates, but incur high computational cost because predictions require sampling weight distributions and multiple forward passes. The Probabilistic Forward Pass (PFP) offers a highly efficient approximation to Stochastic Variational Inference (SVI) by assuming Gaussian-distributed weights and activations, enabling fully analytic uncertainty propagation and replacing sampling with a single deterministic forward pass. We present an end-to-end pipeline for training, compiling, optimizing, and deploying PFP-based BNNs on embedded ARM CPUs. Using the TVM deep learning compiler, we implement a dedicated library of Gaussian-propagating operators for multilayer perceptrons and convolutional neural networks, combined with manual and automated tuning strategies. Ablation studies show that PFP consistently outperforms SVI in computational efficiency, achieving speedups of up to 4200x for small mini-batches. PFP-BNNs match SVI-BNNs on Dirty-MNIST in accuracy, uncertainty estimation, and OOD detection while greatly reducing compute cost. These results highlight the potential of combining Bayesian approximations with code generation to enable efficient BNN deployment on resource-constrained systems.
item.dc:creator: Bernhard Klein, Falk Selker, Hendrik Borras, Sophie Steger, Franz Pernkopf, Holger Fr\"oning

item.title: Redundancy Meets Synergy: Dependency-aware Expert Selection for MoE via Submodular Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.00558v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models effectively scale model capacity through sparse activation, their deployment is often bottlenecked by prohibitive memory requirements. Extracting a compact subset of experts presents a promising solution. However, existing expert selection heuristics predominantly rely on Top-k ranking, which isolates the evaluation of individual experts and ignores the intricate inter-expert dependencies introduced by the MoE gating network. In this paper, we propose DS-MoE, a theoretically grounded framework that redefines expert selection via difference-of-submodular (DS) optimization. By analyzing the second-order Taylor expansion of the loss degradation, we reveal functional duality within expert combinations: redundancy (where experts encode overlapping representations) and synergy (where experts provide complementary error cancellation). To navigate this duality, we mathematically decouple redundancy reduction from synergy maximization by formulating the selection objective as a DS function. Furthermore, we devise a tailored majorization-minimization (MM) algorithm with provable monotonicity guarantees to efficiently identify the optimal expert subset. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DS-MoE effectively preserves indispensable expert combinations, achieving superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art baselines.
item.dc:creator: Zheng Lin, Shaoke Fang, Yuxin Zhang, Jinfeng Xu, Zihan Fang, Zhe Chen, Wei Ni, Jun Luo, Symeon Chatzinotas
